summary: Defines an interim solution allowing a combined user and infrastructure ENUM implementation in e164.arpa as a national choice. The interim approach is to be deprecated once the long-term solution is in place.

eli5.summary: Until a separate address book for phone companies exists, this note lets them share the regular one. It is a temporary fix that should go away later.

questions: what is combined user and infrastructure enum
can carriers use e164.arpa for enum
subtitle: A temporary solution to let carriers share the public telephone numbering database.

tldr.problem: Carriers need a database of which phone numbers they serve and where to send calls, but the existing ENUM system was designed only for end-user phone numbers, not for carrier-to-carrier routing.
tldr.mechanism: This document defines a temporary workaround: create a parallel branch inside the e164.arpa DNS tree for infrastructure ENUM by inserting an 'i' marker at the country code level, following a simple algorithm that differs from standard ENUM only in that one step.
tldr.outcome: Countries can immediately deploy infrastructure ENUM for carrier routing without waiting for a new global DNS zone, with an easy migration path to the long-term solution when available.

today: RFC 5527 defines the interim solution that allows countries to deploy infrastructure ENUM immediately. The long-term solution (RFC 5526) creates a separate zone, and RFC 5527 provides a smooth migration path to transition from the interim to the permanent solution.

sections.title: ENUM and Carrier Routing
sections.content:
ENUM (E.164 Number Mapping) transforms telephone numbers into domain names so the DNS can answer the question: for phone number +1-555-1234, what services are available?

ENUM was defined to handle User ENUM—letting individual users publish where to reach them. However, carriers also need ENUM: when a call arrives at one carrier destined for a phone served by another, the originating carrier needs to know where to send the call. This is Infrastructure ENUM.

The existing e164.arpa tree is not well suited to both purposes at once. They need different delegation structures, different DNS record types, and different security models. A carrier (the "carrier-of-record") publishes a URI saying where to send calls, separate from any URIs the end-user has published.
sections.eli5: ENUM is like phonebook entries in the DNS. The current phonebook was made for customers publishing their own numbers. Phone companies need their own separate phonebook to route calls between carriers.

sections.title: The Interim Algorithm
sections.content:
Standard ENUM transforms a number like +44 2079460123 into a domain name by removing non-digits, placing dots between each digit, reversing the order, and appending ".e164.arpa", yielding a query for "3.2.1.0.6.4.9.7.0.2.4.4.e164.arpa".

The interim Infrastructure ENUM solution uses a modified algorithm: determine the POSITION parameter based on the country code length, build a list of digits, insert the letter "i" at the POSITION in the list, then reverse and append ".e164.arpa". The key difference is that single step: inserting "i" after the first N digits.

For example, +44 2079460123 (a 2-digit country code) becomes "3.2.1.0.6.4.9.7.0.2.i.4.4.e164.arpa" instead of the standard ENUM "3.2.1.0.6.4.9.7.0.2.4.4.e164.arpa". The "i" branch isolates Infrastructure ENUM queries from User ENUM.
sections.eli5: The algorithm is almost the same as regular ENUM, except you insert an 'i' in the right place. This creates a separate branch in the DNS for carrier lookups.

sections.title: Finding the Right Position
sections.content:
The POSITION parameter depends on the phone number's country code, which varies in length from 1 to 4 digits. The RFC provides a specific algorithm: if the number starts with 1 or 7, POSITION is 1; if it is in a list of 2-digit country codes, POSITION is 2; special handling applies to network codes like 883, 881, 882, and 878.

The algorithm is based on ITU-T allocations current as of 2007. Since the ITU-T no longer allocates 1-digit or 2-digit country codes (they are all taken), and new allocations only happen rarely, this table is considered very stable. Countries that split or new allocations would require updating the algorithm, but such events are rare enough that a centralized algorithm remains practical.
sections.eli5: Different countries have phone code numbers of different lengths. You have to know how many digits to count before inserting the 'i'.

sections.title: Transitioning to the Long-Term Solution
sections.content:
This interim solution is intentionally temporary. The long-term solution, described in RFC 5526, creates a new global DNS zone apex for Infrastructure ENUM (not in e164.arpa). When countries start moving to the long-term solution, they will place a DNAME (Delegation Name) record at the "i" branch pointing to their location in the new zone.

This allows clients using the interim algorithm to be automatically redirected without code changes. All DNS systems querying for Infrastructure ENUM must fully support DNAME records and correctly handle synthesized CNAMEs they generate. Once migration is complete and all systems have moved, the interim branch can be removed.
sections.eli5: When a better system is ready, phone companies can put a redirect sign at the old location pointing to the new one, and everything still works.

sections.title: Privacy and Security Considerations
sections.content:
Publishing Infrastructure ENUM information raises privacy concerns: it reveals which numbers are in service and who controls them. The RFC recommends fully unrolling allocated number ranges (publishing entries for every possible number in the range) rather than publishing only numbers in use. This prevents mining attempts to determine which specific numbers are active.

The information exposed should mirror number-range allocation (public information already) but no more. URIs published should not disclose end-user identity; using the E.164 number itself or an anonymized ID in the URI (e.g., sip:+441632960084@example.com) prevents leaking personally identifiable information.
sections.eli5: Publishing the list could reveal which numbers are real. The fix: publish all numbers in the range, so there is no difference between fake and real ones.
